title: Roman construction: brick-faced concrete
source: J.-P. Adam, Roman Building: Materials and Techniques (1994)
text: Most Roman buildings of the imperial period were built of opus caementicium (concrete) faced with fired brick (opus testaceum) or small stones (opus reticulatum), then plastered and painted. Facades of insulae were often left in exposed brick or covered in ochre or white stucco.

title: Insulae: Roman apartment blocks
source: Regionary Catalogues (4th c.); G. Hermansen, Ostia: Aspects of Roman City Life (1982)
text: The 4th-century Regionary Catalogues list about 46,000 insulae and 1,790 domus in Rome. Insulae had 3 to 5 floors, shops (tabernae) with wide arched openings on the ground floor, wooden or brick balconies (maeniana), small windows with wooden shutters or panes of mica/glass, and low-pitched roofs of terracotta tiles (tegulae and imbrices). Height was legally limited to about 20 m.

title: Tabernae: ground-floor shops
text: Tabernae were single-room shops opening to the street through a wide doorway closed at night with wooden boards, often with a masonry counter, a back room and a wooden mezzanine for sleeping.

title: Domus: town houses of the wealthy
source: Wallace-Hadrill, Houses and Society in Pompeii and Herculaneum (1994)
text: A domus was arranged around an atrium with a central impluvium and a garden peristyle; rooms included the tablinum (office), triclinium (dining room with three couches) and cubicula (bedrooms). Floors were mosaic or opus sectile, walls painted with frescoes in red, ochre, black and white.

title: Roof tiles
text: Roman roofs used flat tegulae with flanges covered by semi-cylindrical imbrices, fired terracotta in orange-red to brown; roof pitch was low, about 15 to 25 degrees.

title: Colours of the city
source: general archaeology of Rome and Ostia
text: Typical colours: travertine and marble in cream and white for monuments, red-brown brick, ochre, yellow and pink stucco for houses, orange-red terracotta roofs, green bronze, gilding on important roofs and statues.

title: State of Rome in 476
source: R. Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City 312-1308 (1980)
text: In 476 the great monuments still stood and the Senate still met in the Curia, but the population had fallen from about a million in the 2nd century to perhaps a few hundred thousand. Many insulae stood empty and decayed, gardens and vegetable plots spread inside the walls, and maintenance depended on irregular imperial or royal funding.

title: Sacks of Rome
text: Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in 410 and by the Vandals in 455, who stripped bronze and the gilded roof tiles of the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. The buildings were looted rather than demolished.

title: Theoderic's restorations
text: Under the Ostrogothic king Theoderic (493-526) officials repaired the city walls, aqueducts, the Theatre of Pompey and the Palatine palaces, and a budget from the wine tax funded the upkeep of imperial buildings. Theoderic visited Rome in 500 and stayed on the Palatine.

title: Spolia and lime burning
text: From the 5th century marble from abandoned buildings was reused (spolia) in churches, and statues and architectural pieces were burned in lime kilns (calcariae) set up near the monuments, a practice that grew through the early Middle Ages.

title: Early Christian churches
source: R. Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae
text: Churches of the 4th-5th centuries were basilicas: a tall nave with clerestory windows, lower side aisles separated by reused columns, a semicircular apse with mosaics, a timber roof covered with tiles, plain brick exteriors and often a colonnaded atrium in front. Bell towers (campanili) were added only from the 8th-9th centuries.

title: Temples converted to churches
text: Temple conversions began later: the Pantheon became Santa Maria ad Martyres in 609, and Santi Cosma e Damiano was installed in the library of the Temple of Peace in 527. In 476 most temples were closed but standing.

title: The Colosseum in late antiquity
text: The Flavian Amphitheatre was repaired after earthquakes in 443 and 484 under the prefects; venationes (animal hunts) continued until about 523. Its four storeys had Tuscan, Ionic and Corinthian half-columns and a Corinthian attic with windows; the south side collapsed only in the earthquake of 1349.

title: Circus Maximus
text: Chariot races in the Circus Maximus continued into the 6th century; the last recorded races were held under the Ostrogothic king Totila in 549. The spina carried obelisks, shrines and turning posts (metae).

title: The Palatine palace
source: Domus Flavia and Domus Augustana excavations
text: The palace on the Palatine built by Rabirius for Domitian remained the official imperial residence; western emperors and later Odoacer and Theoderic used it. The Domus Flavia had the Aula Regia (throne hall), the Basilica, the Lararium, a peristyle with an octagonal maze fountain, and the Coenatio Iovis dining hall.

title: Aqueducts
text: Eleven aqueducts supplied Rome. They worked in 476; during the siege of 537 the Ostrogoths cut them, and Belisarius set up floating mills on the Tiber to grind grain.

title: Floating mills on the Tiber
text: Floating mills were two boats moored in the current with a water wheel between them driving millstones in a hut on deck; they were anchored below bridges where the current was strongest, and they remained in use on the Tiber for centuries.

title: Markets
text: Food was sold in the Forum Boarium (cattle market), Forum Holitorium (vegetable market), the macella and at stalls with cloth awnings along streets and porticoes; amphorae of wine and oil, baskets of vegetables, fish from the Tiber and bread were common goods.

title: Animals inside the city
source: early medieval descriptions; the later name Campo Vaccino
text: As the population fell, sheep, goats and cattle grazed in open areas between the monuments; by the Middle Ages the Roman Forum was called Campo Vaccino, the cow field.

title: Trees of Rome
source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History; Roman garden archaeology
text: Trees typical of ancient Rome: stone pine (Pinus pinea) with umbrella crown and edible pine nuts, Mediterranean cypress near tombs and in gardens, olive, laurel (sacred to Apollo), plane trees in porticoes for shade, fig, myrtle and box hedges in gardens.

title: Stone pine
source: Flora of Italy; Pliny, Natural History 16
text: Pinus pinea grows 12-25 m tall with a straight trunk clear of branches for most of its height, thick reddish-brown bark in plates, and a flat umbrella-shaped crown of dark green needles; its cones yield pine nuts eaten since antiquity.

title: Mediterranean cypress
text: Cupressus sempervirens forms a narrow column 10-25 m tall, dark green all year; Romans associated it with mourning and planted it by tombs and in formal gardens.

title: Interior decoration
text: Rich interiors had marble wall revetment in coloured panels (giallo antico yellow, pavonazzetto white with purple veins, porphyry red, serpentine green), opus sectile floors of geometric marble inlay, coffered or vaulted ceilings, bronze candelabra and oil lamps, couches (lecti) for dining, folding stools and wooden chests; modest homes had painted plaster, mosaic or beaten-earth floors and wooden furniture.

title: Lighting
text: Light came from terracotta and bronze oil lamps, candelabra holding lamps, and braziers; windows were small and often closed with shutters, with glass panes in richer buildings.

title: Roman Forum in 476
text: The Forum Romanum still had its paved square, honorific columns and statues, the Curia, the basilicas Julia and Aemilia (damaged in 410 and repaired), and the temples of Saturn, Castor and Vesta; the last monument added there was the Column of Phocas in 608.

title: Bridges
source: Platner and Ashby, Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
text: Stone arched bridges crossing the Tiber in the city included the Pons Aemilius, Pons Fabricius and Pons Cestius to the Tiber Island, and the Pons Aurelius; the Pons Sublicius was traditionally of wood.
